questions.question: Name the elements with the symbols Ca, Br, I and Ne.
questions.modelAnswer: Calcium, bromine, iodine and neon.
markingPoints: Calcium, bromine, iodine and neon.

questions.question: Write the symbols for sodium, magnesium, chlorine and potassium.
questions.modelAnswer: Na, Mg, Cl and K.
markingPoints: Na, Mg, Cl and K.

questions.question: Name the compounds Na₂O, MgCl₂ and CaCO₃. State how you can tell from each formula that it contains more than one element.
questions.modelAnswer:
Na₂O is sodium oxide; MgCl₂ is magnesium chloride; CaCO₃ is calcium carbonate.
Each formula contains symbols for two or more different elements, showing that it is a compound.
markingPoints: Na₂O is sodium oxide; MgCl₂ is magnesium chloride; CaCO₃ is calcium carbonate.
Each formula contains symbols for two or more different elements, showing that it is a compound.

questions.question: Define a compound.
questions.modelAnswer: A substance made from two or more different elements chemically bonded together.
markingPoints: A substance made from two or more different elements chemically bonded together.

questions.question: Define a mixture.
questions.modelAnswer: Two or more substances that are not chemically bonded together.
markingPoints: Two or more substances that are not chemically bonded together.

questions.question: Define an atom.
questions.modelAnswer: The smallest particle of an element that can exist.
markingPoints: The smallest particle of an element that can exist.

questions.question: Define an element.
questions.modelAnswer: A substance made of only one type of atom.
markingPoints: A substance made of only one type of atom.

questions.question: State one difference between a compound and a mixture.
questions.modelAnswer: In a compound, the elements are chemically bonded. In a mixture, the substances are not chemically bonded and can be separated by physical methods.
markingPoints: In a compound, the elements are chemically bonded. In a mixture, the substances are not chemically bonded and can be separated by physical methods.

questions.question: A student says, ‘When iron and sulfur are mixed, a new substance has formed.’ Explain why this is incorrect. Then state what is different after iron and sulfur have reacted to form iron sulfide.
questions.modelAnswer:
A mixture of iron and sulfur contains the original substances; they are not chemically bonded and retain their own properties.
Iron and sulfur can be separated from the mixture by a physical method such as a magnet.
After reacting, iron sulfide is a compound: iron and sulfur are chemically bonded in fixed proportions and have new properties.
markingPoints: A mixture of iron and sulfur contains the original substances; they are not chemically bonded and retain their own properties.
Iron and sulfur can be separated from the mixture by a physical method such as a magnet.
After reacting, iron sulfide is a compound: iron and sulfur are chemically bonded in fixed proportions and have new properties.

questions.question: Balance the equation for magnesium reacting with oxygen and explain what the equation shows about atoms. __Mg + __O₂ → __MgO
questions.modelAnswer:
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
It shows the same number of each type of atom before and after the reaction.
Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.
markingPoints: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
It shows the same number of each type of atom before and after the reaction.
Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.

questions.question: Name the method used to obtain sodium chloride from salt solution.
questions.modelAnswer: Crystallisation or evaporation.
markingPoints: Crystallisation or evaporation.

questions.question: Name the method used to separate crude oil into fractions.
questions.modelAnswer: Fractional distillation.
markingPoints: Fractional distillation.

questions.question: Name the method used to separate ethanol and water.
questions.modelAnswer: Fractional distillation.
markingPoints: Fractional distillation.

questions.question: Name the method used to separate ink dyes.
questions.modelAnswer: Paper chromatography.
markingPoints: Paper chromatography.

questions.question: Name the method used to separate insoluble sand from water.
questions.modelAnswer: Filtration.
markingPoints: Filtration.

questions.question:
A particle model uses ○ for oxygen atoms and ● for carbon atoms.
Box A contains ○○, ○○ and ○○.
Box B contains ●○○, ●○○ and ●○○.
Box C contains ●, ○○ and ●○○.
Part (a): Identify A, B and C as an element, compound or mixture.
Part (b): Justify each answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
A is an element because it contains one type of atom.
B is a pure compound because every particle contains carbon and oxygen atoms chemically joined in the same ratio.
C is a mixture because different particles are present and are not all chemically joined to one another.
markingPoints: A is an element because it contains one type of atom.
B is a pure compound because every particle contains carbon and oxygen atoms chemically joined in the same ratio.
C is a mixture because different particles are present and are not all chemically joined to one another.

questions.question: Explain why fractional distillation, rather than filtration, can separate a mixture of ethanol and water.
questions.modelAnswer:
Both liquids pass through filter paper, so filtration cannot separate them.
They have different boiling points.
Heat the mixture, the lower-boiling component vaporises more readily, then condense and collect it.
markingPoints: Both liquids pass through filter paper, so filtration cannot separate them.
They have different boiling points.
Heat the mixture, the lower-boiling component vaporises more readily, then condense and collect it.

questions.question: A mixture contains sand and dissolved sodium chloride. Describe how to obtain dry samples of both substances.
questions.modelAnswer:
Filter: sand remains as residue.
Wash with distilled water and dry.
Heat the filtrate gently to evaporate some water, cool to crystallise sodium chloride, filter and dry the crystals.
markingPoints: Filter: sand remains as residue.
Wash with distilled water and dry.
Heat the filtrate gently to evaporate some water, cool to crystallise sodium chloride, filter and dry the crystals.

questions.question: A student tries to separate dissolved sodium chloride from water by filtration. Explain why this will not work, then name a method that would produce dry sodium chloride.
questions.modelAnswer:
Dissolved sodium chloride particles pass through the filter paper with the water, so filtration cannot separate them.
Evaporate some water to concentrate the solution, then allow crystals to form and dry the crystals.
Evaporation to dryness is also acceptable when crystals are not required.
markingPoints: Dissolved sodium chloride particles pass through the filter paper with the water, so filtration cannot separate them.
Evaporate some water to concentrate the solution, then allow crystals to form and dry the crystals.
Evaporation to dryness is also acceptable when crystals are not required.

questions.question: A salt solution contains dissolved sodium chloride and water. Describe how to obtain pure water by simple distillation and explain why the salt does not collect in the receiver.
questions.modelAnswer:
Heat the salt solution so that water evaporates.
Pass the water vapour through a condenser, where it cools and condenses.
Collect the liquid water in the receiver.
Sodium chloride has a much higher boiling point and does not evaporate with the water, so it remains in the flask.
markingPoints: Heat the salt solution so that water evaporates.
Pass the water vapour through a condenser, where it cools and condenses.
Collect the liquid water in the receiver.
Sodium chloride has a much higher boiling point and does not evaporate with the water, so it remains in the flask.

questions.question: An ion has 17 protons, 18 electrons and 20 neutrons. State its symbol including mass number and charge, and explain each part.
questions.modelAnswer:
Atomic number 17 identifies chlorine.
Mass number = 17 + 20 = 37
One extra electron gives charge −1, so ³⁷₁₇Cl⁻.
markingPoints: Atomic number 17 identifies chlorine.
Mass number = 17 + 20 = 37
One extra electron gives charge −1, so ³⁷₁₇Cl⁻.

questions.question: State the relative mass, charge and location of a neutron.
questions.modelAnswer: Relative mass 1; charge 0; in the nucleus.
markingPoints: Relative mass 1; charge 0; in the nucleus.

questions.question: State the relative mass, charge and location of a neutron.
questions.modelAnswer: Mass 1; charge 0; nucleus.
markingPoints: Mass 1; charge 0; nucleus.

questions.question: State the relative mass, charge and location of a proton.
questions.modelAnswer: Relative mass 1; charge +1; in the nucleus.
markingPoints: Relative mass 1; charge +1; in the nucleus.

questions.question: State the relative mass, charge and location of an electron.
questions.modelAnswer: Relative mass very small (about 1/1836); charge -1; in shells/energy levels around the nucleus.
markingPoints: Relative mass very small (about 1/1836); charge -1; in shells/energy levels around the nucleus.

questions.question: State the relative mass, charge and location of an electron.
questions.modelAnswer: Very small mass; charge −1; shells/energy levels around the nucleus.
markingPoints: Very small mass; charge −1; shells/energy levels around the nucleus.

questions.question: An ion of chlorine has atomic number 17, mass number 37 and charge 1−. Determine its numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons. Explain each value.
questions.modelAnswer:
17 protons because atomic number = proton number.
20 neutrons because 37 − 17 = 20.
18 electrons because a neutral chlorine atom has 17 electrons and gaining one electron gives a 1− charge.
markingPoints: 17 protons because atomic number = proton number.
20 neutrons because 37 − 17 = 20.
18 electrons because a neutral chlorine atom has 17 electrons and gaining one electron gives a 1− charge.

questions.question:
An atom has radius 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and its nucleus has radius 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ m.
Part (a): Calculate how many times larger the atomic radius is.
Part (b): If the nucleus were represented by a 1 cm ball, calculate the model atom’s radius.
questions.modelAnswer:
Ratio = 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 10⁻¹⁴ = 10⁴ = 10 000.
Model radius = 1 cm × 10 000 = 10 000 cm = 100 m.
markingPoints: Model radius = 1 cm × 10 000 = 10 000 cm = 100 m.

questions.question: Explain why a scientific model may be changed even when the earlier model was useful.
questions.modelAnswer:
Models are simplified explanations based on available evidence.
New observations that the model cannot explain require it to be modified or replaced.
Usefulness does not make a model permanently true.
markingPoints: Models are simplified explanations based on available evidence.
New observations that the model cannot explain require it to be modified or replaced.
Usefulness does not make a model permanently true.

questions.question: Calculate the relative atomic mass of element X. X-63 has 69.2% abundance and X-65 has 30.8% abundance.
Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties.
questions.modelAnswer: They have the same number of electrons and the same electronic structure. Chemical properties depend on the outer-shell electrons.
markingPoints: They have the same number of electrons and the same electronic structure. Chemical properties depend on the outer-shell electrons.

questions.question: Describe how evidence from several independent experiments increases confidence in an atomic model.
questions.modelAnswer:
Different methods test different predictions and have different limitations.
Consistent results are less likely to be due to one apparatus error, bias or chance, so confidence increases.
markingPoints: Different methods test different predictions and have different limitations.
Consistent results are less likely to be due to one apparatus error, bias or chance, so confidence increases.

questions.question: Explain how the alpha-scattering results led Rutherford to replace the plum-pudding model.
questions.modelAnswer:
Examples: iron in the Haber process.
Nickel in hydrogenation of alkenes/vegetable oils.
Vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process.
Manganese dioxide for hydrogen peroxide decomposition.
Any two correct linked examples.
markingPoints: Examples: iron in the Haber process.
Nickel in hydrogenation of alkenes/vegetable oils.
Vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process.
Manganese dioxide for hydrogen peroxide decomposition.
Any two correct linked examples.

questions.question: For ²⁴₁₂Mg and ²⁶₁₂Mg, state what is the same and different and calculate the neutron number of each isotope.
questions.modelAnswer:
Both have 12 protons and, if neutral, 12 electrons.
They are the same element.
Neutrons: 24−12=12 and 26−12=14.
markingPoints: Both have 12 protons and, if neutral, 12 electrons.
They are the same element.

questions.question: Explain how the results of the alpha-scattering experiment led scientists to replace the plum-pudding model.
questions.modelAnswer:
Most alpha particles passed through, showing atoms are mostly empty space.
Some were deflected, showing positive charge and mass are concentrated.
Very few rebounded, showing a tiny, dense nucleus.
The evidence contradicted diffuse positive charge in the plum-pudding model.
markingPoints: Most alpha particles passed through, showing atoms are mostly empty space.
Some were deflected, showing positive charge and mass are concentrated.
Very few rebounded, showing a tiny, dense nucleus.
The evidence contradicted diffuse positive charge in the plum-pudding model.

questions.question:
Describe how the atomic model changed from Dalton’s model to the modern nuclear model.
Include Thomson, Rutherford’s alpha-scattering evidence, Bohr and Chadwick.
questions.modelAnswer:
Dalton: solid indivisible spheres.
Thomson discovered electrons and proposed the plum-pudding model: negative electrons in diffuse positive charge.
Rutherford: most alpha particles passed through, so atoms are mostly empty space.
Some deflected, so positive charge/mass is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
Very few rebounded, so the nucleus is small and dense.
Bohr proposed electrons in fixed energy levels.
Chadwick discovered neutrons in the nucleus.
markingPoints: Dalton: solid indivisible spheres.
Thomson discovered electrons and proposed the plum-pudding model: negative electrons in diffuse positive charge.
Rutherford: most alpha particles passed through, so atoms are mostly empty space.
Some deflected, so positive charge/mass is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
Very few rebounded, so the nucleus is small and dense.
Bohr proposed electrons in fixed energy levels.
Chadwick discovered neutrons in the nucleus.

questions.question:
In an alpha-scattering experiment, most alpha particles pass straight through gold foil, some are deflected and about 1 in 10 000 rebounds.
Part (a): Explain the three conclusions drawn from these observations.
questions.modelAnswer:
Most pass through → atom is mostly empty space.
Some deflect → positive charge is concentrated in a nucleus and repels positive alpha particles.
Very few rebound → nucleus is extremely small, dense and contains most of the atom’s mass.
markingPoints: Most pass through → atom is mostly empty space.
Some deflect → positive charge is concentrated in a nucleus and repels positive alpha particles.
Very few rebound → nucleus is extremely small, dense and contains most of the atom’s mass.

questions.question: Rutherford expected alpha particles to pass through the plum-pudding atom. Explain why the rare large deflections caused the model to be rejected.
questions.modelAnswer:
Diffuse positive charge could not exert the concentrated repulsion needed for large deflections.
Rare rebounds showed most mass and positive charge occupy a tiny dense nucleus, so the plum-pudding model was inconsistent with evidence.
markingPoints: Diffuse positive charge could not exert the concentrated repulsion needed for large deflections.
Rare rebounds showed most mass and positive charge occupy a tiny dense nucleus, so the plum-pudding model was inconsistent with evidence.

questions.question: Explain why a sodium atom has no overall charge.
questions.modelAnswer: It has equal numbers of protons and electrons. The positive charges of the protons balance the negative charges of the electrons.
markingPoints: It has equal numbers of protons and electrons. The positive charges of the protons balance the negative charges of the electrons.

questions.question: Define atomic number. Two atoms each have 8 protons but have different numbers of neutrons. State whether they are the same element and name the relationship between them.
questions.modelAnswer:
Atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus.
They are the same element because elements are defined by their proton number.
They are isotopes of the same element because they have different numbers of neutrons.
markingPoints: Atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus.
They are the same element because elements are defined by their proton number.
They are isotopes of the same element because they have different numbers of neutrons.

questions.question: A neutral sodium atom has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons.
questions.modelAnswer: 11 protons; 12 neutrons; 11 electrons.
markingPoints: 11 protons; 12 neutrons; 11 electrons.

questions.question: An atom has 12 protons and 10 electrons. State its charge and write the symbol of the ion formed. Explain how the charge arises.
questions.modelAnswer:
The atom is magnesium, so the ion is Mg²⁺.
It has two more protons than electrons.
The two extra positive charges give an overall charge of 2+.
markingPoints: The atom is magnesium, so the ion is Mg²⁺.
It has two more protons than electrons.
The two extra positive charges give an overall charge of 2+.

questions.question: Explain why an atom has no overall charge.
questions.modelAnswer: An atom has the same number of positively charged protons as negatively charged electrons, so the charges balance.
markingPoints: An atom has the same number of positively charged protons as negatively charged electrons, so the charges balance.

questions.question: Write the electron arrangement of calcium and state the ion it forms.
markingPoints: Ca²⁺.

questions.question: Write the electron arrangement of chlorine and state the ion it forms.
markingPoints: Cl⁻.

questions.question: Write the electron arrangement of oxygen and state the ion it forms.
markingPoints: O²⁻.

questions.question: Write the electron arrangement of sodium and state the ion it forms.
markingPoints: Na⁺.

questions.question: An atom has electron arrangement 2,8,3. State its period and group, predict the ion formed and explain how it forms.
questions.modelAnswer:
Period 3.
Group 3 
Loses three outer electrons to obtain a full outer shell.
Forms a 3+ ion.
markingPoints: Period 3.
Group 3
Loses three outer electrons to obtain a full outer shell.
Forms a 3+ ion.

questions.question: Explain why successive ionisation energies provide evidence that electrons occupy shells.
questions.modelAnswer:
A large jump occurs after all electrons in an outer shell are removed.
The next electron is closer to the nucleus, less shielded and more strongly attracted, so much more energy is required.
markingPoints: A large jump occurs after all electrons in an outer shell are removed.
The next electron is closer to the nucleus, less shielded and more strongly attracted, so much more energy is required.

questions.question: State the maximum number of electrons in each of the first three shells.
questions.modelAnswer: First shell: 2; second shell: 8; third shell: 8.
markingPoints: First shell: 2; second shell: 8; third shell: 8.

questions.question: State the electron arrangement of magnesium. Draw, or describe precisely, a shell diagram for magnesium showing its electrons in shells.
questions.modelAnswer:
Electron arrangement: 2,8,2.
The shell diagram has 2 electrons in the first shell, 8 in the second shell and 2 in the outer shell.
markingPoints: Electron arrangement: 2,8,2.
The shell diagram has 2 electrons in the first shell, 8 in the second shell and 2 in the outer shell.

questions.question: Element X has isotopes X-63 (69.2%) and X-65 (30.8%). Calculate its relative atomic mass.
Explain how Mendeleev organised his periodic table and why scientists later accepted it.
questions.modelAnswer:
He ordered mainly by relative atomic mass but changed the order where chemical properties required it.
Placed elements with similar properties in columns.
Left gaps for undiscovered elements.
Predicted properties of missing elements.
Later discoveries closely matched his predictions, providing evidence for the table.
markingPoints: He ordered mainly by relative atomic mass but changed the order where chemical properties required it.
Placed elements with similar properties in columns.
Left gaps for undiscovered elements.
Predicted properties of missing elements.
Later discoveries closely matched his predictions, providing evidence for the table.

questions.question: Explain how an element’s position in the periodic table relates to its electronic structure.
questions.modelAnswer: The group number gives the number of electrons in the outer shell. The period number gives the number of occupied electron shells.
markingPoints: The group number gives the number of electrons in the outer shell. The period number gives the number of occupied electron shells.

questions.question: Explain how the modern periodic table is organised.
questions.modelAnswer: Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number. Elements in the same group have similar properties. Rows are called periods.
markingPoints: Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number. Elements in the same group have similar properties. Rows are called periods.

questions.question: Mendeleev placed tellurium before iodine even though tellurium had the greater atomic weight. Explain why he did this and why it was a strength of his table.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mendeleev prioritised chemical properties and placed tellurium with elements that had similar properties, and iodine with the halogens.
This preserved useful groups even when strict atomic-weight order did not fit.
It showed that the arrangement was based on a pattern in properties, not just a list of masses.
markingPoints: Mendeleev prioritised chemical properties and placed tellurium with elements that had similar properties, and iodine with the halogens.
This preserved useful groups even when strict atomic-weight order did not fit.
It showed that the arrangement was based on a pattern in properties, not just a list of masses.

questions.question: State where metals and non-metals are found in the periodic table.
questions.modelAnswer: Metals are on the left and centre of the periodic table. Non-metals are on the right.
markingPoints: Metals are on the left and centre of the periodic table. Non-metals are on the right.

questions.question: Compare the physical properties of metals and non-metals.
questions.modelAnswer: Metals are usually good conductors, strong and malleable. Non-metals are usually poor conductors and, when solid, are brittle.
markingPoints: Metals are usually good conductors, strong and malleable. Non-metals are usually poor conductors and, when solid, are brittle.

questions.question: Compare the typical ion formation of metals and non-metals.
questions.modelAnswer: Metals lose electrons to form positive ions. Non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions. The number gained or lost gives a full outer shell.
markingPoints: Metals lose electrons to form positive ions. Non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions. The number gained or lost gives a full outer shell.

questions.question: Compare Newlands' and Mendeleev's approaches to arranging the elements. Explain why Mendeleev's table became more useful.
questions.modelAnswer: Both arranged elements mainly by atomic weight. Newlands used a repeating pattern and sometimes placed unlike elements together. Mendeleev left gaps and changed the order when properties showed this was needed. His predictions for undiscovered elements were later confirmed, supporting his table.
markingPoints: Both arranged elements mainly by atomic weight. Newlands used a repeating pattern and sometimes placed unlike elements together. Mendeleev left gaps and changed the order when properties showed this was needed. His predictions for undiscovered elements were later confirmed, supporting his table.

questions.question: Explain why noble gases are monatomic and very unreactive.
questions.modelAnswer: They have full outer electron shells. They do not need to gain, lose or share electrons, so they are very unreactive. They exist as single atoms rather than bonded molecules.
markingPoints: They have full outer electron shells. They do not need to gain, lose or share electrons, so they are very unreactive. They exist as single atoms rather than bonded molecules.

questions.question: Explain why argon is used in filament lamps and helium is used in balloons.
questions.modelAnswer:
Argon is unreactive because it has a full outer shell, so it does not react with the hot filament.
Helium is unreactive and less dense than air, so balloons rise and it does not burn.
markingPoints: Argon is unreactive because it has a full outer shell, so it does not react with the hot filament.
Helium is unreactive and less dense than air, so balloons rise and it does not burn.

questions.question: Describe and explain the trend in boiling point and reactivity down Group 0.
questions.modelAnswer:
Noble gases are very unreactive because they have full outer electron shells.
Boiling points increase down the group because atoms are larger/have more electrons, so intermolecular attractions between atoms are stronger and more energy is required to overcome them.
markingPoints: Noble gases are very unreactive because they have full outer electron shells.
Boiling points increase down the group because atoms are larger/have more electrons, so intermolecular attractions between atoms are stronger and more energy is required to overcome them.

questions.question: A mass spectrum gives relative abundances of 75% for mass 35 and 25% for mass 37. Calculate the relative atomic mass.
Helium has only two electrons. Explain why it is nevertheless very unreactive.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first electron shell is full when it contains two electrons.
Helium therefore has a full outer shell and does not need to gain, lose or share electrons.
markingPoints: The first electron shell is full when it contains two electrons.
Helium therefore has a full outer shell and does not need to gain, lose or share electrons.

questions.question: Lithium reacts with oxygen and separately with chlorine. Write a word equation for each reaction and explain why lithium forms similar compounds to sodium.
questions.modelAnswer:
lithium + oxygen → lithium oxide.
lithium + chlorine → lithium chloride.
Lithium and sodium are both Group 1 metals with one outer electron, so they form +1 ions and have similar chemical properties.
markingPoints: lithium + oxygen → lithium oxide.
lithium + chlorine → lithium chloride.
Lithium and sodium are both Group 1 metals with one outer electron, so they form +1 ions and have similar chemical properties.

questions.question: State the pH of the solution made when a Group 1 metal reacts with water.
questions.modelAnswer: Alkaline; pH greater than 7.
markingPoints: Alkaline; pH greater than 7.

questions.question: State two observations when sodium reacts with water.
questions.modelAnswer: It floats/moves and fizzes. It may melt into a ball.
markingPoints: It floats/moves and fizzes. It may melt into a ball.

questions.question: Write the balanced symbol equation for sodium reacting with water.
questions.modelAnswer: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.
markingPoints: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.

questions.question: Write the general word equation for a Group 1 metal reacting with water.
questions.modelAnswer: metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen.
markingPoints: metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen.

questions.question: Explain why Group 1 metals become more reactive down the group.
questions.modelAnswer:
Each atom has one outer electron.
Down the group there are more shells, greater distance and more shielding.
Attraction between the nucleus and outer electron is weaker, so the electron is lost more easily and reactivity increases.
markingPoints: Each atom has one outer electron.
Down the group there are more shells, greater distance and more shielding.
Attraction between the nucleus and outer electron is weaker, so the electron is lost more easily and reactivity increases.

questions.question: The boiling points of lithium, sodium and potassium are 1342, 883 and 759 °C. Describe the trend and predict a reasonable boiling point for rubidium.
questions.modelAnswer:
Boiling point decreases down the group.
A prediction below 759 °C, with sensible extrapolation (about 650–700 °C), is supported.
Exact value not required.
markingPoints: Boiling point decreases down the group.
A prediction below 759 °C, with sensible extrapolation (about 650–700 °C), is supported.
Exact value not required.

questions.question: Each fluorine atom has seven outer electrons. Explain how two fluorine atoms form an F₂ molecule and state the total number of electrons in the molecule.
questions.modelAnswer: Each fluorine atom shares one electron to make one shared pair. This forms a covalent bond and gives each atom a full outer shell. An F₂ molecule has 18 electrons in total.
markingPoints: Each fluorine atom shares one electron to make one shared pair. This forms a covalent bond and gives each atom a full outer shell. An F₂ molecule has 18 electrons in total.

questions.question: Explain why Group 1 metals become more reactive down the group.
questions.modelAnswer: There are more electron shells. The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.
markingPoints: There are more electron shells. The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.

questions.question: Explain why potassium reacts more vigorously with water than sodium.
questions.modelAnswer: Potassium has more electron shells. Its outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.
markingPoints: Potassium has more electron shells. Its outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.

questions.question: Potassium reacts with water. State the products and write a balanced symbol equation.
questions.modelAnswer: Potassium hydroxide and hydrogen are formed. 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂.
markingPoints: Potassium hydroxide and hydrogen are formed. 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂.

questions.question: Predict and explain the relative reactivity of potassium and lithium.
questions.modelAnswer:
Potassium is more reactive.
Its outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so nuclear attraction is weaker and the electron is lost more easily.
markingPoints: Potassium is more reactive.
Its outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so nuclear attraction is weaker and the electron is lost more easily.

questions.question: Describe the trend in state and colour of the halogens down Group 7.
questions.modelAnswer: They become darker in colour and have higher melting and boiling points. At room temperature, fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid.
markingPoints: They become darker in colour and have higher melting and boiling points. At room temperature, fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid.

questions.question: Explain why halogens become less reactive down Group 7.
questions.modelAnswer: Atoms have more electron shells down the group. The outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded. The nucleus attracts an incoming electron less strongly.
markingPoints: Atoms have more electron shells down the group. The outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded. The nucleus attracts an incoming electron less strongly.

questions.question: Chlorine reacts with magnesium and with hydrogen. State the formula of each product and identify which product is ionic. Explain your choice.
questions.modelAnswer: Magnesium chloride is MgCl₂. Hydrogen chloride is HCl. MgCl₂ is ionic because magnesium transfers electrons to chlorine, forming Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. HCl is covalent because hydrogen and chlorine share electrons.
markingPoints: Magnesium chloride is MgCl₂. Hydrogen chloride is HCl. MgCl₂ is ionic because magnesium transfers electrons to chlorine, forming Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. HCl is covalent because hydrogen and chlorine share electrons.

questions.question: Iodine solution is added to sodium bromide solution. State whether a reaction occurs and explain using Group 7 reactivity.
questions.modelAnswer:
No reaction.
Iodine is below bromine and is less reactive, so it cannot displace bromide ions from sodium bromide.
markingPoints: No reaction.
Iodine is below bromine and is less reactive, so it cannot displace bromide ions from sodium bromide.

questions.question:
Chlorine water is added separately to potassium bromide and potassium iodide solutions.
Bromine water is added to potassium chloride solution.
Part (a): Predict the outcomes, give colour observations.
Part (b): Write ionic equations for reactions that occur.
questions.modelAnswer:
Chlorine displaces bromide: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂
Solution becomes orange.
Chlorine displaces iodide: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂

questions.question:
